92.title: Vessantara gives
92.hook: the generous prince gives away the kingdom's rain-bringing white elephant and is exiled
92.howItsDone: In Thailand, Laos and Cambodia the Vessantara story is recited in full at a yearly temple festival, often in a single day, and it is taught as the great story of dana, generosity.

A bag of old clothes left at the donation bin is an easy gift: things nobody wanted anyway. The good jacket is harder. A free Saturday. The last of something. Today's story lives in that harder place. It's the last of the five hundred and forty-seven Jatakas in the Pali collection, and the longest. In parts of Southeast Asia it is recited aloud at temple festivals, sometimes all in one day. It's about a prince who gives away the thing nobody wanted him to give.

segments.voice: Vessantara is the crown prince of the Sivi kingdom, and from childhood he loves to give. The story says he wanted to give even his own heart or eyes if someone asked. His kingdom owns a treasure: a magnificent white elephant, and wherever it goes, the rain comes. Then envoys arrive from a neighboring land, Kalinga, where the rains have failed and the fields are cracking. They ask for the elephant. Vessantara, sitting on its back, pours water over their hands, the old sign of a gift, and gives it to them. Picture the city the next morning. Their rain has just walked out of the gate. The people are furious and demand his exile, and his father, the king, gives in. So Vessantara leaves the palace for a mountain in the forest, and his wife Maddi and their two small children choose to go with him. On the way out he gives away even more: his chariot, his horses. They walk the last part on foot, he and Maddi each carrying a child. Why does this story come last? Tradition says Vessantara is the Buddha's last human life before the one in which he awakens, and that here he completes the perfection of giving, dana. It isn't told as a sensible budget. It's giving taken as far as it can go. And the story doesn't hide the cost: a whole city angry, a family without a home. Tomorrow, the cost gets harder still.

93.title: Vessantara's children
93.hook: he gives away even his children before the reunion; Buddhists have debated this story for centuries
93.howItsDone: Theravada Buddhists hear the whole Vessantara story at festivals and in sermons, and teachers and listeners openly discuss its hardest scenes, as the tradition's own texts already do.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Vessantara gives, the rain elephant handed away and the prince sent into the forest. Your line: generosity costs.

Some stories you finish and think: wait. That can't be right. Every tradition has a few of these, and the grown-up thing isn't to skip them. It's to sit with them. Today's part of the Vessantara story is one of those. Buddhist teachers, kings, monks and ordinary listeners have been arguing about it for about two thousand years. So today, no tidying up. First the story, then the argument.

segments.voice: In the forest, the family lives in a simple hermitage. One day, while Maddi is out gathering fruit, an old brahmin named Jujaka arrives. His young wife wants servants, and he's come to ask Vessantara for his children, Jali and Kanhajina. The children hide in a lotus pond. Their father calls them out, and he gives them. Jujaka ties their hands and drives them off. The story doesn't soften it: the children cry, and Vessantara weeps. Then the god Sakka arrives in disguise and asks for Maddi. He gives her too, and Sakka at once gives her back. The ending is a reunion. Jujaka wanders to the capital, the grandfather king buys the children back, Jujaka dies of overeating, and the whole family returns home in joy. But the questions don't go away. In the Questions of King Milinda, an old dialogue, the king asks the monk Nagasena straight out: wasn't this cruel to the children and the wife? Nagasena defends the gift. The father knew the grandfather would ransom them, he says, and the gift was made for the sake of awakening. Other Buddhists across the centuries have been less comfortable, and modern listeners, including many Buddhists, raise the same worry about the wife and children who had no say. Some read the story as a picture of total non-attachment, never a rule for how to raise a family. Some say it shows how costly the path to becoming a Buddha is meant to be. Others simply say it hurts. The tradition doesn't hide the argument. It keeps retelling the story, and keeps arguing.

94.title: Temiya the silent prince
94.hook: a prince pretends to be mute for sixteen years rather than rule by punishment
94.howItsDone: The Temiya story is told as the first of the ten great Jatakas, and in Thailand and elsewhere it's painted on temple walls; Buddhists link it with the perfection of renunciation.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Vessantara's children, and the argument Buddhists have had about them for centuries. Your line: the tradition argues too.

A meeting ends, and one person never said a word. Was it wisdom? Was it fear? From the outside, the two look exactly the same. Today's story is about a silence so long and so stubborn that everyone decided the silent one was broken. He wasn't. He was choosing. It's the Temiya Jataka, number 538, the first of the ten long Jatakas that close the collection, and it starts with a baby on a king's lap.
screen: `WISDOM OR FEAR?` → `FROM OUTSIDE, THEY LOOK THE SAME.` → `A BABY ON A KING'S LAP.`

segments.voice: The baby is Temiya, the long-awaited son of the king of Benares. Still only an infant, he sits on his father's lap while the king judges prisoners, and he watches his father order terrible punishments. And the story says the baby remembers: in a past life he was a king too, and the harsh judgments he handed down led him to long suffering afterward. He's terrified. He does not want this throne. A goddess who lives in the royal parasol gives him advice: pretend you can't speak, can't hear, can't walk. So he does. For sixteen years. The court tries everything to catch him out: sweets he could reach for, frightening noises, fire, snakes. Every test, the story says, he stays still. Finally the advisers tell the king this son is bad luck, and the king orders him taken out and buried. The charioteer drives him to the forest and starts to dig. Then Temiya stands up, walks, lifts the chariot, and speaks. He tells the charioteer why he kept silent, and he chooses the life of a forest ascetic. In the end his parents and much of the kingdom come out and follow him. In the tradition, this life is linked with nekkhamma, renunciation: leaving behind the power that would have made him cruel. His silence wasn't weakness, or sulking. It was a refusal. He would not say the words that condemn.

95.title: Mahajanaka's swim
95.hook: shipwrecked, he swims seven days without seeing land, because effort is never wasted
95.howItsDone: Buddhists tell the Mahajanaka story as an example of viriya, effort, and in Theravada countries such as Thailand it is retold in books, art and temple murals.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Temiya, the silent prince, sixteen years without a word. Your line: silence can be a choice.

A thesis in its third draft. A recovery that moves an inch a week. A job hunt on its fortieth application. Some projects have no shore in sight, and at some point a reasonable voice asks: what's the point? You can't even see the end. Today's story, the second of the ten long Jatakas, asks that question in the middle of the ocean. A prince, a sinking ship, and a goddess who wants to know why he's still swimming.
screen: `A PROJECT WITH NO SHORE IN SIGHT.` → `WHAT'S THE POINT?` → `THE MIDDLE OF THE OCEAN.`

segments.voice: Mahajanaka is a prince born in exile. His father, the king of Mithila, was killed by his own brother, and his mother fled while pregnant. When the boy grows up and learns the truth, he decides to win back what was lost, so he joins a trading ship bound for a far country to make his fortune. Out at sea, the ship breaks apart. The others weep and pray and drown. Mahajanaka, the story says, does something practical. He eats his fill, soaks his clothes in oil against the cold water, climbs the mast, and leaps as far out as he can, clear of the wreck and the sea creatures. Then he swims. Seven days, the story says, with no land in sight. On the seventh day a sea goddess named Manimekhala appears above the waves and asks him, in effect: why bother? There's no shore. You'll die out here. His answer is the heart of the story. A person who makes the effort, even if they die trying, is free from blame, he says, and giving up guarantees failure, while effort at least gives a chance. Effort is never wasted. Moved by his answer, she lifts him out of the sea and carries him to Mithila, where, in time, he becomes king. In the tradition, this life shows the perfection of viriya: effort, energy, courage that keeps going. Not effort because success is certain. Effort because it's the only part that's yours.

96.title: Camp 2 close: the whole life
96.hook: from the palace to the sal trees, from the hare to the prince: stories that teach by being remembered
96.howItsDone: Buddhists learn the Buddha's life through retelling: in sermons, temple murals, children's books and festival plays, the same stories are told again and again until they're known by heart.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Mahajanaka's swim, seven days in open water, and a goddess asking why. Your line: swim anyway.

A queen asleep, dreaming of a white elephant: that's where this camp began, on day twenty-two. You didn't know then who Channa was, or Kanthaka, or Sujata. You'd never heard of Kisa Gotami or the man with the finger garland. Now, if someone at dinner said the Buddha just sat under a tree and got enlightened, you could tell them about the six years first. The handful of beans. The bowl that floated upstream. That's what stories do. They don't argue. They move in and stay. Today, the last day of the stories, walk the whole life once more, from the palace to the sal trees.
screen: `A QUEEN, A DREAM, A WHITE ELEPHANT.` → `THEY MOVE IN AND STAY.` → `THE LAST DAY OF THE STORIES.`

segments.voice: Walk it with me. A child born in a grove at Lumbini, and an old sage who weeps because he won't live to hear him teach. A prince named Siddhattha, the one whose aim succeeds, in three palaces built to keep sorrow out. Then four sights through the gate: an old man, a sick man, a dead man, and a calm wanderer. A son named Rahula. A sleeping palace, one look back, a horse named Kanthaka, and hair cut with a sword. Two teachers, then six hard years with five companions, down to a handful of beans, until he remembered a quiet afternoon under a rose-apple tree. Sujata's rice. Eight handfuls of grass, a vow, Mara's army, and a hand touching the earth. Dawn, and a new word: Buddha, awake. Then the Deer Park, the wheel set turning, Kondañña seeing, the sangha growing, and the women who asked to join and were ordained. The hard stories: a murderer who stopped, a mother with a mustard seed, Patacara who lost everything and found her feet. Eighty years, dipa, Cunda's meal, two sal trees, and the last words: strive on. Then the Jataka, the lives before, told by the tradition as the long road here: sasa, the hare in the moon, the deer who saved his betrayer, the prince who gave until it hurt, the prince who stayed silent, the prince who swam. Stories don't teach the way lists do. They teach by being remembered at the right moment. You don't just know about him now. You know him.

97.title: The four phrases
97.hook: may you be safe, may you be happy, may you be healthy, may you live with ease
97.howItsDone: One way Buddhists practice metta is by repeating short wishes, silently or aloud, for themselves and others; the wording varies by teacher and school, and Theravada communities often chant the Metta Sutta itself.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Jataka, the whole life, from the palace to the sal trees, and the lives before. Your line: you know him now.

In Buddhist teaching, loving-kindness isn't only a feeling you wait for. People practice it on purpose, with words, again and again, the way you'd practice a scale on a piano. Metta was the first word on this path, on day one, before any of the stories. Back then it was a word. Now it gets hands and feet. Camp three, the practices, begins here, and for the next sixty days the path is about doing: the sitting, the walking, the precepts, the giving, the chanting, the holy days. And it starts with metta.
screen: `PRACTICED LIKE A SCALE.` → `BACK TO THE FIRST WORD: METTA.` → `FROM STORIES TO PRACTICE.`

segments.voice: Here are the four phrases this path uses, in a common modern form. May you be safe. May you be happy. May you be healthy. May you live with ease. Each one is a wish, not a demand. Safe: free from danger, inside and out. Happy: a settled gladness, not a party. Healthy: in body and mind. At ease: life not being a constant struggle. Now, an honest note. These exact four lines are modern, and teachers word them a little differently. What's old is the wish itself. The Metta Sutta, a text Theravada Buddhists chant, wishes that all beings be happy and secure, that their hearts be glad. The Path of Purification, an old manual by the monk Buddhaghosa, gives phrases of its own. So the phrases are a tool, like a handrail: something for the mind to lean on when the feeling isn't there yet. And that's the part people find surprising: you don't have to feel warm to begin. You say the words slowly and sincerely, and you notice what happens. Some days, warmth. Some days, nothing. Some days, resistance. All of it counts. Over the next ten days you'll send these wishes out in widening circles: to yourself, a helper, a friend, a stranger, a difficult person, and finally everyone. Today, just the four lines.
screen: `SAFE, HAPPY, HEALTHY, AT EASE.` · `THE WORDS ARE MODERN.` · `THE WISH IS OLD.` · `A HANDRAIL, NOT A FEELING.` · then, large: `MAY YOU BE AT EASE.`

segments.voice: Silently and slowly, say the four phrases once, with a pause and a breath after each: may you be safe, may you be happy, may you be healthy, may you live with ease. Don't aim them at anyone yet; just notice what they do in the body, softening, nothing, a little resistance, and whatever shows up is fine. When the words are done, rest in the quiet after them.
Metta. Loving-kindness: the old practice behind the four phrases, may you be safe, happy, healthy, and at ease.
Your line: may you be at ease. The last of the four phrases, and the one to keep. Ninety-seven days, and counting.

98.title: Starting with yourself
98.hook: the old manuals begin metta with oneself, the easiest proof that everyone wants to be happy
98.howItsDone: In many Buddhist metta practices, especially those following the Visuddhimagga, practitioners begin by wishing themselves well before extending the wish to others.

segments.voice: Yesterday: metta, the four phrases, safe, happy, healthy, at ease. Your line: may you be at ease.

Quick test. Say to a friend: I hope you have a good day. Easy. Now say it to yourself, out loud: I hope I have a good day. For a lot of people, that second one feels strange. Embarrassing, even. Selfish. As if kindness only goes outward. So here's a surprise from the old Buddhist manuals. When they teach metta step by step, the very first person they tell you to wish well is not your mother, not a teacher, not the world. It's you.
screen: `I HOPE YOU HAVE A GOOD DAY.` → `I HOPE I HAVE A GOOD DAY.` → `THE FIRST PERSON IS YOU.`

segments.voice: The manual is the Visuddhimagga, the Path of Purification, written by the monk Buddhaghosa in Sri Lanka around the fifth century. Its ninth chapter, on loving-kindness, says to begin by wishing yourself well: may I be happy, may I be free from suffering. Why start there? Not because you're the most important person in the room. Almost the opposite. When you wish yourself well, you notice something plain: I want to be happy. I don't want to suffer. Use that as your example, the manual says. Everyone else wants exactly the same thing, just as much. Your own wish is the easiest proof. The manual backs this up with a teaching from the Pali texts. King Pasenadi and Queen Mallika, the story goes, admit to each other that nobody is dearer to them than themselves. The Buddha doesn't scold them. He answers with a verse, in substance: search every direction, and you won't find anyone dearer to a person than their own self; since each one holds themselves that dear, whoever loves themselves should harm no one. So starting with yourself isn't the selfish shortcut. It's the doorway. Metta for yourself alone isn't the goal, the manual says; it's where you learn what the wish feels like, so you can hand it on. And on a hard day, the voice in your head that says you don't deserve kindness is exactly the voice this practice answers. You count too.
screen: `THE PATH OF PURIFICATION, CHAPTER NINE.` · `MAY I BE HAPPY.` · `YOUR WISH IS THE PROOF.` · `NOBODY DEARER THAN ONESELF.` · then, large: `YOU COUNT TOO.`

segments.voice: Rest your hands somewhere comfortable, maybe one over your heart, and offer the phrases to yourself slowly, with space between: may I be safe, may I be happy, may I be healthy, may I live with ease. If it feels awkward, that's normal; let the awkwardness be there too. If it helps, picture yourself as a small child and say the words to them.
Atta. Oneself: the old manuals begin metta with you, since your own wish to be happy shows you what everyone wants.
Your line: you count too. It closes a week that began with the last long Jatakas and the end of the story camp, and ends with metta, step by step. That's day ninety-eight.
